name: LuaJIT Remake (Deegen)
baseline: PUC Lua 5.1 interpreter (also compared with the LuaJIT interpreter)
workload: 46 Lua benchmark scripts in luabench/ (fannkuch, nbody, binary-trees, scimark, deltablue, richards, json and others), geometric mean of 5 repeats, interpreter mode only, GC disabled in all compared implementations.
claimed_speedup: Interpreter is 185% faster than the official PUC Lua 5.1 interpreter (about 2.85x) and 34.6% faster than LuaJIT's interpreter, geometric mean over the benchmarks (README).
compiler_and_flags: Built with 'python3 ljr-build make release' inside a Docker image (ubuntu:20.04 with a patched LLVM/Clang, see dockerfile/); exact compile flags and the PUC Lua / LuaJIT build flags are not stated in the README.
hardware: Intel Core i7-12700H laptop, 32GB DDR4 (author's machine)
tradeoffs: x86-64 Linux only; Lua 5.1 semantics only; interpreter and runtime use hidden-class tables instead of Lua's hash tables; needs Docker and a patched LLVM to build; JIT tiers are still work in progress; package library (require/module) not implemented.
caveats: Tier B rests on the peer-reviewed Deegen paper (OOPSLA 2026, doi 10.1145/3798246, arXiv 2411.11469) whose existence I saw in search results but could not open (egress blocked); search snippets of the paper quote 2.79x over PUC Lua and 1.31x over the LuaJIT 2.1 interpreter, and a baseline JIT at 4.60x over PUC Lua and about 33% slower than LuaJIT's optimizing JIT (snippet only, not verified). The README numbers come from the author's own laptop; run_bench.sh in the repo only runs luajitr, so the PUC Lua and LuaJIT baseline runs are not scripted in the repo. The README states GC is not implemented and GC was turned off for the baselines for fairness, which flatters allocation-heavy benchmarks. Last commit is 19 months old and focused on the DFG JIT backend. The README's 34.6% and 185% figures differ from the paper's snippet figures (README may predate paper revisions).
found_via: WebSearch 'Deegen LuaJIT Remake compiler-compiler framework fast VM interpreter faster than PUC Lua LuaJIT interpreter' (also surfaced by the seed query 'fast interpreter dispatch design paper faster than CPython Lua')

name: PrimJS
workload: Octane benchmark suite (15 sub-benchmarks, Octane score version 9) run on both engines.
claimed_speedup: Octane overall score 3735 vs 2904 for QuickJS (about 28% higher). Per test: RayTrace 2751 vs 1273, EarleyBoyer 4270 vs 2284, NavierStokes 4166 vs 2640, PdfJS 6642 vs 4236, Crypto 1844 vs 1349; CodeLoad (16992 vs 18137) and MandreelLatency (9587 vs 9680) are slightly lower.
compiler_and_flags: gn build with enable_quickjs_debugger=false target_cpu=arm64 target_os=mac is_debug=false enable_optimize_with_O2=true; snapshot, compatible_mm and tracing GC at defaults; compiler name not stated (gn default toolchain).
hardware: Apple M1 Max, 64GB RAM, macOS Sonoma 14.0
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; engine of the Lynx cross-platform framework
tradeoffs: Built for Lynx: ES2019 only; replaces QuickJS reference counting with a tracing garbage collector; adds a template interpreter with stack caching and register optimizations plus snapshot support; Chrome DevTools Protocol integration. Not a standalone drop-in CLI.
caveats: First-party benchmark; single machine (ARM64 macOS) and single suite; compiler not named so tier A is borderline (benchmark suite, build arguments and CPU are all public). Baseline is QuickJS, not V8, so it is not faster than V8; it is a lighter-weight embedded engine. No memory or startup comparison given on the page. Octane is deprecated and favours older JS patterns.
found_via: Follow-up on the WebSearch 'JavaScript interpreter engine C++ faster than QuickJS github benchmark results V8 jitless startup memory paper' (result list included primjs); opened lynx-family/primjs README and docs/benchmark.md

name: Shed Skin
language: Python (transpiler) generating C++; runtime library in C++
baseline: CPython 3.14 (headline claim); CPython 3.10.6 and 3.11.0 in the sieve timing
workload: Over 80 non-trivial example programs (more than 25,000 lines) in the examples directory, plus a sieve example with n=100000000 timed against several Python implementations.
claimed_speedup: Typical speedup of 1-100x over CPython 3.14 (average 20x, median 12x) across the examples. Sieve n=100000000: CPython 3.10.6 13.4 s, CPython 3.11.0 11.4 s, Shed Skin 0.9.9 1.9 s (--int32) and 1.8 s (--int32 --nowrap --nobounds), about 6-7x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Shed Skin flags --int32 --nowrap --nobounds for the fastest sieve run; C++ compiler and optimization flags for the 80-program measurement not stated on the page.
license: GPL-3.0 (compiler); MIT/Expat, BSD-3-Clause and BSL-1.0 for the C++ runtime library; examples individually licensed
tradeoffs: Accepts only a restricted, implicitly statically typed Python 3 subset: about 25 stdlib modules, no external libraries, no nested functions or variable argument counts; depends on the Boehm GC; programs often need refactoring; default integers are int64 (use --int32 for narrower).
caveats: First-party numbers with no CPU model or compiler version on the page; the 1-100x range includes programs chosen by the project and individual speedups are only in an image. The sieve table compares different tools at different CPython versions; README shows a separate comparison of Shed Skin and PyPy against CPython 3.10 (git tag performance_comparison) as an image only. Compared with Numba the README notes Numba defaults to int64, so int width affects the comparison.
found_via: Direct fetch of github.com/shedskin/shedskin after the WebSearch 'Python compiler paper open source speedup over CPython github Codon Pythran Cinder Pyston benchmarks' (Python-to-native compilers); its README also supplied the PyPy and Nuitka numbers below

name: Codon
baseline: CPython (python3 on the README's example machine, version not stated)
workload: README examples: recursive fib(40), and a NumPy pi estimate over 500 million random points (Codon's own native NumPy implementation vs NumPy under CPython).
claimed_speedup: fib(40): 17.979 s under python3 vs 0.2756 s with 'codon run -release' (about 65x, derived from page data). NumPy pi example: 2.25 s vs 0.43 s (about 5x, derived from page data). README: typical speedups over vanilla Python are on the order of 10-100x or more on a single thread.
compiler_and_flags: codon run -release; CPython version, build and C++/LLVM toolchain not stated.
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time compiler for a Python-like language, not a drop-in CPython replacement: static typing with different semantics (fixed-width ints), partial standard-library and package support (other packages via a python bridge), no dynamic features that defeat static typing; adds native multithreading without a GIL and GPU support.
caveats: README numbers are two micro examples on an unstated machine. The peer-reviewed Codon paper (CC 2023) and the exaloop.io benchmark page report broader suites against CPython, PyPy and C++, but both were unreachable (egress blocked), so tier B evidence was not verified. The 100x end of the claim comes from workloads where CPython's interpreter overhead dominates.
found_via: WebSearch 'Python compiler paper open source speedup over CPython github Codon Pythran Cinder Pyston benchmarks' (surfaced the Codon CC'23 paper); opened exaloop/codon README

name: GraalPy
baseline: CPython (current release at the time of the chart; version not stated in text)
workload: Official Python Performance Benchmark Suite (pyperformance), run on both interpreters, both installed through pyenv; result shown as a chart.
claimed_speedup: GraalPy is geomean ~4x faster than CPython on pyperformance (README text); pure Python code often faster after JIT compilation; C extension performance near CPython.
tradeoffs: Runs on the JVM/GraalVM (also as a standalone binary and embeddable in Java); README says it passes about 85% of CPython's tests, and C extension performance is near CPython but varies; the README text itself notes JIT compilation is needed to reach the speedup, so warmup applies.
caveats: Chart image only; the per-benchmark table, CPU model, JVM build and the CPython build (PGO/LTO or not) are not on the page. pyperformance geomeans hide large per-benchmark spread and the warmup cost. First-party (Oracle) claim; the GraalPy/Truffle peer-reviewed papers were not opened.
found_via: Direct fetch of oracle/graalpython README while following the Truffle/Graal line after the seed query 'fast interpreter dispatch design paper faster than CPython Lua'

name: Pyston
language: C (CPython 3.8.12 fork with a DynASM-based JIT)
workload: Web serving macrobenchmarks (the project's python-macrobenchmarks style suite); micro numbers not given.
claimed_speedup: Pyston full is roughly 30% faster than CPython on web serving macrobenchmarks; Pyston lite (JIT extension module only) roughly 10% faster on macrobenchmarks.
compiler_and_flags: Build documentation mentions LLVM, LTO, PGO and BOLT; flags for the measured numbers not stated.
tradeoffs: Fork of CPython 3.8.12 (full) or an extension module for Python 3.7-3.10 (lite); targets x86 Linux.
caveats: Repository description reads '(No longer maintained)'; last commit 26 months old. Numbers are first-party, rounded, with no hardware, harness or raw data on the opened page; CPython 3.11+ has its own specializing interpreter, so the gap against current CPython is likely smaller (not measured here). Included as a historical design to study (quickening, attribute caching, low-overhead JIT).
found_via: WebSearch 'Python compiler paper open source speedup over CPython github Codon Pythran Cinder Pyston benchmarks' (Pyston named in result); opened pyston/pyston README and commits

name: Nuitka
workload: pystone, best of 100-1000 runs, uncompiled vs compiled with --lto=yes (and --pgo-c); script tests/benchmarks/pystone.py in the repo.
claimed_speedup: Debian Python 2.7 pystone 137497.87 uncompiled vs 460995.20 compiled with LTO (3.35x) and 503681.91 with PGO (3.66x); Nuitka-built Python 2.7: 144074.78 vs 479271.51 (3.49x) and 511247.44 (3.72x).
compiler_and_flags: nuitka --lto=yes --pgo-c (and --static-libpython=yes for the Python 3 variant); C compiler version for the table not stated (README says GCC 5.1+, Clang or MSVC 2022+ supported).
tradeoffs: Compiles Python to C and still depends on a Python runtime; speedups are modest on dynamic code; needs a C compiler; AGPL-3.0 licence (check implications for compiled output).
caveats: The published table is pystone on Python 2.7 only (the README says the Python 3 focus will follow); pystone is a synthetic benchmark and the README adds that real-world gains vary. No CPU model. An independent timing in the Shed Skin README shows Nuitka 0.6.16 at 11.4 s on the sieve example, identical to CPython 3.11.0 (11.4 s) and only slightly faster than CPython 3.10.6 (13.4 s), so gains on other workloads can be near zero.
found_via: WebSearch 'Python compiler paper open source speedup over CPython github Codon Pythran Cinder Pyston benchmarks' (Nuitka in the compiled-Python comparison study); opened Nuitka README

name: mypyc
baseline: CPython (interpreted mypy and annotated Python code)
workload: Annotated Python modules compiled to C extensions; mypy itself compiled with mypyc as the flagship example.
claimed_speedup: Existing code with type annotations is often 1.5x to 5x faster when compiled; code tuned for mypyc can be 5x to 10x faster; compiled mypy achieved a 4x performance improvement over interpreted Python (mypyc introduction).
stars_or_usage: 20.7k stars (mypy repository; mypyc lives in the mypyc/ subdirectory); mypy itself is compiled with mypyc per the docs
tradeoffs: Restricts some dynamic Python features (see differences_from_python in the docs); requires type annotations to see gains; output is a C extension built with a C compiler and runs under CPython.
caveats: Ranges are described in prose with no benchmark table, hardware or harness on the opened page; the 4x for mypy is the project's own anecdotal figure. The repo reports mypy under mypyc; mypyc is a subproject, not a standalone repository.
found_via: Direct fetch of mypyc/doc/introduction.rst after the WebSearch 'Python compiler paper open source speedup over CPython github Codon Pythran Cinder Pyston benchmarks' listed compiled-Python tools (mypyc named in the empirical study)

name: YJIT (CRuby)
workload: ruby-bench micro and macro benchmarks (30k_ifelse, 30k_methods, fib, activerecord, liquid-render, optcarrot, railsbench, lee, binarytrees, nbody, fannkuchredux and others), interpreter time over YJIT time after warmup.
claimed_speedup: Example table in the ruby-bench README (marked 'results below not up to date'): fib 3.18x, 30k_ifelse 5.30x, 30k_methods 6.57x, optcarrot 1.33x, activerecord 1.19x, liquid-render 1.19x, railsbench 1.07x, lee 1.08x, binarytrees 1.14x, nbody 1.00x, fannkuchredux 1.00x.
stars_or_usage: Ships in CRuby (ruby/ruby 23.8k stars); the sibling ZJIT is in the same repository
tradeoffs: Uses more memory than the interpreter (executable memory plus metadata); supported on x86-64 and arm64/aarch64 macOS, Linux and BSD; requires a Rust toolchain to build; warmup needed.
caveats: The numbers opened are an explicitly outdated example table in the benchmark repo README, with no Ruby version, CPU or flags. The peer-reviewed papers (VMIL 2021 'YJIT: A Basic Block Versioning JIT Compiler for CRuby' and MPLR 2023 'Evaluating YJIT's Performance in a Production Context') are linked from doc/jit/yjit.md, but dl.acm.org was blocked, so tier B was not verified; search snippets quote 15-19% speedups on large real-world benchmarks and 20% on railsbench, 39% on liquid, 37% on activerecord for the earliest version (snippet only). Repo is ruby/ruby as a whole, so stars and license describe all of CRuby.
found_via: WebSearch 'YJIT basic block versioning JIT CRuby paper speedup over MRI interpreter benchmarks github'; opened doc/jit/yjit.md and the yjit-bench README

name: LuaJIT
workload: Single numeric program run by the DNS/benchmark-language suite (all languages print 7051.571...), wall time of one run.
claimed_speedup: LuaJIT 2.1.1694442928 0.81 s vs Lua 5.4.2 3.69 s (and luac 5.4.2 3.27 s), about 4.6x faster (derived from page data); equal to C (GCC 7.2.0) at 0.78 s.
compiler_and_flags: Windows batch run-benchmark.bat; Lua and LuaJIT build flags not stated.
stars_or_usage: 5.8k stars (GitHub mirror of the official repository)
tradeoffs: Lua 5.1 based (not Lua 5.3/5.4 semantics); the GitHub repository is a mirror of the official LuaJIT git repository.
caveats: Evidence is an independent but tiny single-workload comparison (a repo with 26 stars) without compiler flags. LuaJIT's own performance page (luajit.org/performance.html) was blocked. A second source: the luajit-remake README (https://github.com/luajit-remake/luajit-remake) gives its interpreter as 185% faster than PUC Lua 5.1 and 34.6% faster than LuaJIT's interpreter, which implies LuaJIT's interpreter alone is about 2.1x faster than PUC Lua 5.1 (derived from page data, JIT disabled). Recorded as a core incumbent that later work (LuaJIT Remake, Pallene, Luau) is measured against.
found_via: WebSearch 'new Lua virtual machine implementation faster than Lua 5.4 benchmark github C++ interpreter register-based speedup' (surfaced DNS/benchmark-language)

name: Wren
baseline: Lua 5.2.3, Ruby 2.0.0p247, Python 3.3.4 / 2.7.5 (and LuaJIT 2.0.2 with JIT disabled as a faster reference)
workload: Method call, DeltaBlue, Binary Trees and Recursive Fibonacci benchmarks from test/benchmark; best of 10 runs, excluding interpreter startup.
claimed_speedup: Method Call: Wren 0.12 s, Ruby 0.20 s, Lua 0.35 s, Python 3 0.78 s. Binary Trees: Wren 0.22 s, Ruby 0.24 s, Python 0.37 s, Lua 0.52 s. Recursive Fibonacci: Wren 0.20 s, Ruby 0.22 s, Lua 0.28 s, Python 0.51 s. DeltaBlue: Wren 0.13 s vs Python 3.3.4 0.48 s (Lua and Ruby not in that chart). LuaJIT 2.0.2 with JIT off is faster on Binary Trees (0.11 s) and Fibonacci (0.10 s).
hardware: MacBook Pro, 2.3 GHz Intel Core i7, 16 GB 1,600 MHz DDR3
tradeoffs: Small class-based scripting language, not source compatible with Lua/Python/Ruby; single-pass compiler to bytecode with a compact object representation (README), no JIT.
caveats: Numbers are about a decade old (Lua 5.2.3, Python 2.7.5/3.3.4, Ruby 2.0.0), so modern Lua 5.4, CPython 3.11+ and Ruby 3.x are not represented; only four micro benchmarks; compiler flags unstated; the author notes LuaJIT with JIT enabled is much faster than all. Benchmark harness is public in test/benchmark.
found_via: Direct fetch of wren-lang/wren doc/site/performance.markdown (design-paper style interpreter write-up) after the seed query 'fast interpreter dispatch design paper faster than CPython Lua'; not surfaced by a search hit

name: LLRT (Low Latency Runtime)
workload: AWS Lambda cold-start round-trip time (init duration plus function duration) of a DynamoDB Put function, ARM, 128MB; results shown as images in the README.
claimed_speedup: Up to over 10x faster startup and up to 2x overall lower cost compared to other JavaScript runtimes on AWS Lambda (README text).
hardware: AWS Lambda ARM, 128MB memory (no CPU model)
tradeoffs: No JIT, so peak compute is far slower than V8 and not recommended for compute-heavy work; partial Node.js API compatibility; ES2023 only; README marks it experimental and for evaluation purposes.
caveats: Only cold-start latency is measured, where QuickJS-based no-JIT startup wins by design; the headline is 'up to over 10x' with the measured numbers only in images; README methodology explains why round-trip time is used instead of Init Duration. Written in Rust, so it is a runtime to adopt, not a C++ library.
found_via: Direct fetch of awslabs/llrt following the WebSearch 'JavaScript interpreter engine C++ faster than QuickJS github benchmark results V8 jitless startup memory paper' (JS engines vs V8)

name: CPython tail-calling interpreter
baseline: CPython computed-goto interpreter loop (same source, default dispatch)
workload: pyperformance suite, CPython built with clang-19, ThinLTO and PGO on AMD64 Ubuntu 22.04; results in a gist linked from the issue.
claimed_speedup: After correction: geomean 3-5% faster on pyperformance. Original claim was a 10% geomean speedup with up to 40% on Python-heavy benchmarks, which the issue now says was artificially boosted by an LLVM 19 compiler bug.
compiler_and_flags: clang-19 (needs Clang 19+ on x86-64 and AArch64), ThinLTO and PGO; PGO is said to be especially crucial for the speedup.
hardware: AMD64 machine, Ubuntu 22.04 (CPU model not on the page)
tradeoffs: Needs Clang 19 or newer (x86-64 and AArch64) and PGO to pay off per the issue.
caveats: Baseline is CPython itself, so this is a delta against the incumbent's previous dispatch, not against another implementation. The headline number was withdrawn by the authors after an LLVM 19 bug was found; the corrected 3-5% geomean is the figure to use,. CPU model absent, so the tier is C.
found_via: WebSearch 'research prototype Python interpreter source code released speedup over CPython 3.12 geometric mean pyperformance paper 2025 github' (surfaced issue #128563)

name: PyPy
language: Python/RPython (meta-tracing JIT generated through a C backend)
workload: Shed Skin's sieve example (n=100000000) run under several Python implementations (third-party table in the Shed Skin README).
claimed_speedup: pypy 3.9.12 5.8 s vs cpython 3.10.6 13.4 s (about 2.3x, derived from page data) and cpython 3.11.0 11.4 s (about 2.0x, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: JIT warmup applies; building from source is described as time-consuming and discouraged; behaviour with CPython C extensions not checked on the opened pages.
caveats: The repository page itself has no numbers (speed.pypy.org and pypy.org were blocked), so this entry rests on a single third-party micro workload with no hardware; the Shed Skin README also has a PyPy-vs-CPython 3.10 chart as an image only. Tier C may undersell PyPy, which has years of public benchmarks (speed.pypy.org) and peer-reviewed tracing JIT papers that I could not open.
found_via: Shed Skin README (opened for the Shed Skin entry) after the WebSearch 'Python compiler paper open source speedup over CPython github Codon Pythran Cinder Pyston benchmarks'

name: Hermes
baseline: JavaScriptCore (React Native's previous default engine); V8 not benchmarked on the opened page
workload: React Native app start-up; the repository page gives no benchmark.
claimed_speedup: No numbers on the opened page: repository description says 'optimized for fast start-up of React Native apps' with ahead-of-time static optimization and compact bytecode.
stars_or_usage: 11.3k stars; default JavaScript engine of React Native
tradeoffs: Described as optimized for fast start-up with ahead-of-time static optimization and compact bytecode; peak throughput versus JIT engines is not claimed on the page.
caveats: Tier D, the single no-number entry: the claim is first-party and unquantified on the page I opened. Search snippets from third-party blogs (Callstack, React Native blog 'Toward Hermes being the Default', blocked here) quote roughly 25-50% TTI improvements, about 40% faster start on iOS than JavaScriptCore and about 26% lower memory (JSC 185 MB vs Hermes 136 MB), but those pages were not opened.
